articles.title: US CPI preview: energy set to lift inflation to 3.7%, core seen steady at 2.4%
articles.description: Wednesday’s report is a direct read on how far the Iran war’s energy shock is feeding into US consumer prices, and a hot energy component would reinforce the link between crude risk and Fed policy. Treasury markets are likely to trade the core number rather than the headline: a soft core would favour the front end and weigh on the dollar, while a firm one would revive October hike pricing that faded after weak payrolls. Gold would likely benefit from a soft core and lower yields. With Brent still above $100 and fresh attacks on Saudi infrastructure, energy-driven inflation risk extends well beyond this release. -- September’s CPI is set to look alarming on the surface and calm underneath, and the Fed has to decide which one to believe. Summary: US September CPI is due Wednesday at 12:30 GMT (8:30 ET), the last inflation report before the Fed’s October 27-28 meeting The market expects headline CPI to rise 0.6% on the month, lifting the annual rate to around 3.7% from 3.4% Core inflation is forecast to slow to around 0.2% on the month, holding at 2.4% annually Energy is expected to jump around 5.5%, led by gasoline, while food stays subdued Odds of an October Fed hike have fallen to around one in four after weak September payrolls, with December still largely priced Fed Chair Warsh speaks in Bangkok early Friday, his final scheduled remarks before the meeting US consumer prices are expected to post their sharpest monthly rise since April when September inflation data is released on Wednesday, driven almost entirely by energy, while underlying inflation is forecast to stay subdued. The market expects headline CPI to climb 0.6% in September, according to Westpac’s calendar, up from 0.4% in August. That would lift the annual rate to around 3.7% from 3.4%, a four-month high. The Cleveland Fed’s inflation nowcast points in the same direction, at about 0.5% for the month and 3.6% on the year. The report is due at 12:30 GMT (8:30 ET). Energy is the main driver. Analysts expect energy prices to rise around 5.5% in the month, led by gasoline, which would be the largest energy contribution since March. In August, gasoline prices were already up more than 27% on a year earlier. Core inflation, which excludes food and energy, is expected to tell a calmer story. Forecasts point to a rise of around 0.2%, slower than August’s 0.3%, keeping the annual core rate at 2.4%. August’s core reading was boosted by a one-off jump in telephone services following a methodology change, and analysts expect volatile items such as hotel prices and used cars to correct. Airfares are the exception, rising as higher jet fuel costs pass through to ticket prices. That split puts the Federal Reserve in an awkward position. The Fed raised its target range to 3.75%-4.00% on September 16, but the odds of a follow-up move at the October 27-28 meeting fell to around one in four after September payrolls showed only 29,000 jobs added. Markets still largely price a December hike. Goldman Sachs had expected one more increase in October, though that view assumed oil would fall towards $85, and Brent remains above $100. A firm core reading alongside the energy-driven headline would likely revive October hike bets, while a soft core would reinforce expectations of a December move. Thursday’s producer prices and retail sales will add to the picture before Fed Chair Kevin Warsh speaks at the IMF meetings in Bangkok early Friday, his last scheduled appearance before the meeting. This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

articles.title: Red flags fly after latest ICE shooting 'puts everyone in a little more danger': expert
articles.description: A former leader of the Department of Homeland Security's Immigration and Customs Enforcement division sounded the alarm on Sunday after immigration agents shot and injured a man they were trying to apprehend in New York while the individual's 5-year-old son was in the car. On Friday, ICE agents shot and injured 28-year-old Oscar Belgal in Brooklyn, New York. Mark Morales of CNN reported on Sunday that the bullet is still lodged in Belgal's neck and his face is still numb from the incident. John Sandweg, former acting director of ICE, sounded the alarm about the incident in a new interview on CNN. He noted that it appeared an office from the Immigration Enforcement Division was responsible for the shooting, which is a team that has historically never conducted the kind of work that the Trump administration is asking them to do now. "In fact, almost every single one of these shootings, it's been that particular unit," Sandweg said. "And so while the Secretary talks about how every agency does undercover operations, that is true, except this unit never historically did this. This is a new phenomenon we've seen in the trump administration. And what concerns former colleagues of mine at ICE and me is that we see this particular unit engaging in tactics that are outside of their experience and outside of their training, and that's reflected in the plans and the tactics and these aggressive uses of force." Sandweg also noted that it will take to stop more ICE shootings from occurring. "The bottom line [is that] we need to see ICE revert back to those tactics that historically they did, which is primarily focusing on people who are already in prison and jail, taking them into custody in a secure environment there," Sandweg said. "And when you do these at-large operations, doing them in a way that's safe and secure, doing it early in the morning outside their residence." "I think we have another political factor here driving a lot of this, and that is these quotas and this pressure that ICE is under to hit certain targets in terms of how many arrests," he continued. "I don't think we should underestimate the role that is playing in pushing these agents to be so aggressive and taking risks that they otherwise wouldn't take." "It's not just risks to the immigrants who are being arrested ... it's a risk to the officers themselves," he added. "These tactics put everyone in a little bit more danger."
